Here's my Short Commentary: The Next Ombudsman: A Test of Integrity—or an Exercise in Irony?

The race for the next Ombudsman is on, and, true to Philippine political tradition, it’s already drenched in intrigue, factional drama, and moral contradictions. Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla, the seemingly and allegedly Marcos Jr.’s administration’s likely “chosen one,” has thrown his hat into the ring. The only problem? He also happens to sit—by law—on the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), the very body that screens and shortlists candidates for the position. Even with his promised inhibition, one cannot help but appreciate the sheer irony: the man helping to choose the next Ombudsman is himself on the list?? Wow! Seriously??

To recap, Ombudsman Samuel Martires’ seven-year term ended on July 27, 2025, and the JBC has transmitted a shortlist of seven names to Malacañang. Whoever President Marcos Jr. chooses will hold office for another seven years. A period that could well shape the accountability architecture of his administration. Among the names are respected jurists and technocrats, but it’s Remulla’s inclusion that has set off alarm bells louder than a siren in a traffic stop.

Senator Imee Marcos has publicly opposed Remulla’s application, alleging he still faces pending cases at the Ombudsman and a disbarment complaint filed by Davao City Mayor Baste Duterte in the Supreme Court. The JBC requires clearance of any administrative or criminal case before endorsement. Remulla himself admitted he’s still waiting for that clearance. Perhaps, in the Philippines, political ambition rarely waits for paperwork.

However, the controversy extends beyond bureaucracy. It’s about independence, or the lack thereof. The Ombudsman is supposed to be and is meant to be the public’s last bastion against abuse of power. Appointing the sitting Secretary of Justice (Boying Remulla), one of the President’s closest political allies, to that role would blur the already thin line between watchdog and lapdog. In a system where political loyalty often trumps institutional integrity, such a move would be less a coincidence than a confirmation.

And then there’s the political backdrop. The Marcos-Duterte rift looms large. Remulla’s potential appointment is being framed as part of a “Plan C” in a supposed campaign of “lawfare” against Vice President Sara Duterte and her allies. Whether or not this conspiracy holds water, the perception alone is enough to turn the selection into a proxy war.

Substantively, Remulla’s record raises eyebrows. His hardline stance on the International Criminal Court’s (ICC) drug war probe, first rejecting, then half-welcoming cooperation, offers a preview of how he might handle politically sensitive cases as Ombudsman. Add to that the active investigations into the multi-billion-peso flood-control corruption scandal, and it’s clear that whoever takes over the office will step directly into a political minefield.

The stakes could not be higher. The Ombudsman’s credibility now hangs by a thread. Will the next appointee restore transparency, or perfect opacity? The Filipino public deserves an independent guardian, not a recycled loyalist.

In the end, Malacañang’s choice will say more about the administration’s conscience than its competence. If the next Ombudsman turns out to be another political ally in robes, we may as well rename the office the “Department of Selective Justice.”

Because in this Marcos Jr. government, irony has long ceased to be a literary device; it has become government policy.
 Folks, the next Ombudsman could either restore trust or rubber-stamp impunity. Guess which one Malacañang prefers? Your guess is as good as mine! 
When the watchdog is also the Palace’s Pitbull, who exactly gets bitten? Folks, I guess, you know the answer to this, right?
